opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few layers to it. The most obvious one is self-preference bias. If you use GPT-4 as the judge, it tends to favor outputs that look like GPT-4 outputs, and the same goes for Claude judging Claude-style responses. So if you're developing a model that was trained on, say, distilled data from one of these systems, you can get an inflated score just because your model has picked up the stylistic quirks the judge likes, not because it's actually better at the task.

Then there are more general biases that have been documented pretty well at this point. Length bias is a big one: judges tend to prefer longer, more verbose answers, even when a shorter answer is more correct or more useful. There's position bias in pairwise comparisons, where the model prefers whichever answer is shown first, or second, depending on the model, so you have to swap the order and average to get anything reliable. And there's a kind of formatting or confidence bias, where an answer with nice bullet points and an authoritative tone gets rated highly even if the content is subtly wrong.

The reason that matters so much is that these evaluations increasingly drive decisions. People pick checkpoints, tune data mixtures, and write papers based on these win rates. If the metric is biased, you end up optimizing for the bias. You train models to be longer, more formatted, more like the judge, and you think you're making progress when you're mostly just gaming the evaluator. It's Goodhart's law in a pretty direct form.

There's also a reproducibility issue that's related. These are closed models that get updated behind an API, so the judge you used six months ago might not be the judge you're using today, and your numbers quietly shift. That makes it hard to compare across papers.

So my view isn't that LLM-as-a-judge is useless. It's actually really valuable, it scales, and it correlates reasonably with human preferences in a lot of settings. But you need to be aware of these biases and control for them: swap positions, control for length, use multiple judges from different model families, and where possible ground things in tasks with verifiable answers, so you're not relying entirely on one model's taste.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-4 tends to favor GPT-4-like outputs and Claude favors Claude-style responses, identifying self-preference bias when either evaluates similar outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we built things like the MTEB leaderboard, or when we did the OLMo and OLMoE work and needed to judge model outputs, this kept coming up. The core issue is that when you use something like ChatGPT or Claude as your judge, you're not getting a neutral measurement. You're getting that model's preferences baked into your evaluation.

There are a few concrete ways this shows up. The most obvious one is self-preference. If GPT-4 is judging outputs, and one of the candidates is GPT-4 or a model distilled from GPT-4 outputs, it tends to rate those higher. The style, the phrasing, the way it structures an answer all look "right" to the judge because that's what it would have written. So you end up rewarding models for imitating the judge rather than for actually being better.

Then there's the stylistic bias. These judges tend to prefer longer responses, responses with more formatting, more bullet points, more hedging. Those things aren't the same as correctness. We've seen cases where a shorter, more precise answer gets rated lower than a verbose one that's actually less accurate. And position bias is real too, where whichever answer appears first, or second, gets a systematic bump depending on the judge.

The deeper problem for me is what this does to the research ecosystem. If everyone optimizes against the same handful of closed judges, the whole field converges toward whatever those models like. And the judges themselves are changing. The GPT-4 you used in your paper six months ago isn't the same model behind the API today, so your numbers aren't even reproducible. That's partly why I care so much about open models and open evaluation. If the judge is open, you can at least inspect it, hold it fixed, and understand what biases you're inheriting.

So I'm not saying never use them. They're incredibly useful, especially for open-ended tasks where there's no clean reference answer. But you have to treat the scores as one noisy signal, cross-check with human evaluation or with tasks that have verifiable answers, and be very careful about reading small differences as real improvements.

r001.rationale: It says a judge such as GPT-4 tends to rate GPT-4 or models distilled from its outputs more highly, identifying self-evaluation bias.

astra-6.text: The concern is that these models aren’t neutral judges. They have preferences for particular writing styles, formatting, or longer answers, and those preferences don’t necessarily reflect whether an answer is actually better. They can also favor outputs from themselves or similar models. So if you use GPT to evaluate everything, you may end up measuring how well a model matches GPT’s preferences rather than how useful or correct it is. And once people optimize against that judge, those biases can become part of what we train models to reproduce.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluator models can favor their own outputs and warns that using GPT as the judge can measure alignment with GPT’s preferences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main concern is that these models aren’t neutral judges. They have preferences for certain styles of responses, and those preferences don’t necessarily line up with correctness or what a user actually wants. A longer, more polished answer might get a higher score even if a shorter answer is just as good or more accurate.

There can also be a preference for outputs that resemble the judge’s own responses. So if you use ChatGPT or Claude as your evaluator, you may end up measuring how well a model matches that particular judge’s preferences rather than how capable it really is. They’re useful for evaluation, but I wouldn’t treat their judgments as ground truth.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT or Claude may favor outputs resembling the judge’s own responses, but it does not clearly identify the specific risk of either model evaluating itself.
